message.content: would it make sense to not take dependency on the dotnet project from the cli and rather pipe it in? like intropy dashboard ... | dotnet run ...

content.text:
It's a reasonable instinct (and very Unix), but I'd keep the exec approach as the default — the pipe works against the dashboard's main use case in a few concrete ways:

**What the pipe costs you**

- **Refresh dies.** The dashboard is a long-running server; a pipe delivers the topology once, at startup. The dev loop this feature exists for — edit the system, click "Refresh topology", see the new graph — would become "kill the server, re-run the pipeline". With exec, the server can re-run the verb on demand; that's the feature the refresh endpoint provides.
- **Multi-system workspaces stop being automatic.** Today the server discovers every `role: system-host` scaffold and queries each one. A pipe carries one document, so you'd need the user to concatenate documents or run one pipeline per system.
- **The direction is awkward.** It would have to be `dotnet run --project <host> -- graph | intropy dashboard -` (topology flowing *into* the CLI), and the user has to remember that incantation per workspace — versus `intropy dashboard` just working.

**What it buys you**

- No dotnet dependency in the Go server, no process execution, no 5-minute timeout/stdout-hygiene handling at runtime — genuinely simpler server code.
- The slow first `dotnet` build happens visibly in the terminal instead of behind a slow first HTTP request.

The dependency worry is also softer than it looks: dotnet is only exercised for the flow view, the catalog and detail views never touch it, and the dashboard's audience is by definition people developing a .NET system — they have the SDK. And the stdout-contract coupling doesn't disappear with a pipe; it just moves from the Go server to the shell.

**If you want the decoupling anyway**, the cheap middle ground is a flag rather than a pipe as the *only* mode: `intropy dashboard --topology <file|->` that reads a pre-produced document (from stdin or a file) and skips exec entirely. That's ~30 lines — a second `topologyProvider` that calls the existing `topology.Decode` — because the provider is already injected as a function for exactly this kind of swap. Refresh would just re-serve the piped document (or be disabled in that mode). Useful for CI screenshots, SDK-less machines, or debugging a hand-edited topology.

My recommendation: keep exec as the default, and add `--topology -` only if one of those scenarios is real for you. Happy to implement the flag if you want it.

# Contributing to intropy CLI

Thank you for your interest in contributing! This document covers the workflow,
standards, and conventions we follow.

## Table of Contents

- [Getting Started](#getting-started)
- [Development Workflow](#development-workflow)
- [Commit Message Convention](#commit-message-convention)
- [Pull Request Process](#pull-request-process)
- [Code Standards](#code-standards)
- [Testing](#testing)
- [Project Conventions](#project-conventions)
- [Reporting Issues](#reporting-issues)

---

## Getting Started

### Prerequisites

- [Go 1.26+](https://go.dev/dl/)
- macOS or Linux (Windows developers: use [WSL 2](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/wsl/install))
- A working Go module cache (`go env GOPATH`)

### Clone and build

```bash
git clone https://github.com/integrio-intropy/intropy-cli.git
cd intropy-cli
make build
```

Or manually:

```bash
go build -o bin/intropy ./cmd/intropy
```

Verify the build:

```bash
./bin/intropy version
# or
make run ARGS="version"
```

### The dashboard SPA (`intropy dashboard`)

`intropy dashboard` serves a local web dashboard. The frontend is a Vite +
React + TypeScript app under [`web/`](web/); its production build (`web/dist`)
is embedded into the Go binary via `//go:embed` (see `web/embed.go`).

A minimal placeholder `web/dist/index.html` is committed so `go build` and
`go test` work **without** a Node toolchain. The real assets are built on
demand — locally with `make web`, and in CI / GoReleaser before the Go build —
and are **not** committed (`web/.gitignore` excludes them).

To build the CLI with the real dashboard embedded:

```bash
make bundle    # = make web && make build
```

Frontend dev loop (hot reload, talks to a running CLI):

```bash
# terminal 1 — the CLI serves the JSON API on :8730
./bin/intropy dashboard --no-browser

# terminal 2 — Vite dev server proxies /api to the CLI
make web-dev   # or: cd web && npm run dev
```

> Note: a local `npm run build` overwrites `web/dist/index.html` and adds
> `web/dist/assets/`. Don't commit the modified index.html — `make web-clean`
> (or `git checkout web/dist/index.html`) restores the placeholder.

The flow view renders each system's declared topology, which the server
obtains by running the system host's `graph` verb (`dotnet run --project
<host> -- graph`). The verb must print the `topology.intropy.io/v1` record as
JSON on stdout (logs go to stderr); the result is cached until the dashboard's
"Refresh topology" action re-runs it.

## Development Workflow

We use a **feature-branch workflow** with pull requests to `main`.

```bash
# Sync your fork
gh repo sync --branch main

# Or manually
git fetch upstream
git rebase upstream/main

# Create a feature branch
git checkout -b feat/short-description
```

### Branch naming

| Prefix | Use for |
|--------|---------|
| `feat/` | New commands, flags, or capabilities |
| `fix/` | Bug fixes |
| `docs/` | README, help text, or code comment changes |
| `refactor/` | Internal restructuring without behavior change |
| `test/` | New or updated tests |
| `chore/` | Dependency updates, tooling, maintenance |

**Examples:** `feat/int-create-dry-run`, `fix/template-archive-paths`, `docs/readme-install`

## Commit Message Convention

We follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) for
automated changelog generation.

```
<type>(<scope>): <description>

[optional body]

[optional footer(s)]
```

**Types:** `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `style`, `refactor`, `test`, `chore`

**Scopes (common):** `int`, `skills`, `oci`, `template`, `cli`, `deps`

**Examples:**

```
feat(int): add --dry-run flag to create

fix(template): handle nested archive paths on extraction

docs(readme): update install instructions for macOS
```

## Pull Request Process

1. **Open a draft PR early** for large or complex changes.
2. **Fill out the PR description** — what changed and why.
3. **Ensure CI passes** — `go test ./...`, `go vet ./...`, and `gofmt` must be green.
4. **Request review** from maintainers.
5. **Address feedback** promptly. Amend commits and force-push to the same branch.

### PR Checklist

- [ ] `make check` passes (fmt, vet, tests)
- [ ] `make ci` passes if you have `golangci-lint` installed (full pipeline)
- [ ] Code is formatted with `gofmt` (or `gofumpt`)
- [ ] `go mod tidy` has been run if imports changed
- [ ] New or changed behavior has tests
- [ ] Command-line changes update help text and README if applicable
- [ ] Commit messages follow the convention above
- [ ] Only relevant files are committed (no `git add .`)
- [ ] No debug code, `fmt.Printf` artifacts, or temporary files

## Code Standards

### Go style

- Follow [Effective Go](https://go.dev/doc/effective_go) and the
  [Go Code Review Comments](https://go.dev/wiki/CodeReviewComments).
- Run `make fmt` (or `gofumpt`) before committing.
- Run `make vet` to catch common mistakes.
- Run `make tidy` after adding or removing imports.

### CLI patterns

This project uses Cobra + Viper. When adding or modifying commands:

- Set `SilenceUsage: true` and `SilenceErrors: true` on the command.
- Return errors from `RunE` — never call `os.Exit()` inside commands.
- Write diagnostic output to `cmd.ErrOrStderr()`, program output to `cmd.OutOrStdout()`.
- Bind flags to Viper with `viper.BindPFlag` for env/config support.
- Use `cobra.ExactArgs`, `cobra.MinimumNArgs`, etc. for argument validation.
- Provide `RegisterFlagCompletionFunc` for flag value completion.

### Error handling

- Return wrapped errors with context: `fmt.Errorf("resolving template: %w", err)`
- Use exit code `2` for usage errors (invalid flags/args), `1` for runtime errors.

## Testing

### Run the test suite

```bash
make test
```

Or manually:

```bash
go test ./...
```

### Run with race detection

```bash
make test-race
```

Or manually:

```bash
go test -race ./...
```

### Key testing patterns

- Test commands by executing them programmatically and capturing output.
- Use `cmd.SetOut(buf)` and `cmd.SetErr(errBuf)` so tests can inspect output.
- Mock OCI registry calls and HTTP transports (e.g. the GitHub template client) — do not hit the network or real registries in tests.
- Each `_test.go` file lives alongside the code it tests.

### Adding tests

- New features **must** include tests.
- Bug fixes **should** include a regression test.
- Table-driven tests are preferred for multiple cases.

## Project Conventions

### Project layout

```
cmd/intropy/          Cobra commands — one file per command + tests
internal/template/    Template download, validation, describe, render
internal/system/      `sys create` — assemble scaffolds into a system host
internal/dashboard/   Local `intropy dashboard`: HTTP server + JSON API
internal/topology/    topology.intropy.io/v1 schema + decoder (host graph verb output)
internal/skill/       skills.json/lockfile, install/update/add, collection cache
internal/skill/oci/   OCI client wrappers, pack/push/pull, references
web/                  Dashboard SPA (Vite + React + TS), embedded via go:embed
```

### Version stamping

Version, commit, and build date are injected at compile time. When testing locally:

```bash
go build -ldflags "\
  -X main.version=dev \
  -X main.commit=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) \
  -X main.date=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" \
  -o bin/intropy ./cmd/intropy
```

### OCI and skills compliance

The `skills` subsystem implements the
[Agent Skills OCI Artifacts Spec](https://github.com/ThomasVitale/agents-skills-oci-artifacts-spec).
When modifying OCI packaging, pulling, or metadata, ensure conformance with the
spec. Changes that affect wire format or artifact structure should be discussed
in an issue first.

## Reporting Issues

Before opening an issue:

1. Search existing issues (open and closed) for duplicates.
2. Use a clear, descriptive title.

A good bug report includes:
- Steps to reproduce
- Expected vs. actual behavior
- Output of `intropy version`
- Environment: OS, Go version (`go version`)
- If applicable: the exact command and flags used

## License

By contributing, you agree that your contributions will be licensed under the
[MIT License](LICENSE).

## Security

If you discover a security vulnerability, **do not open a public issue**.
Email the maintainers directly.

content.text:
Answer: **the system-host template needs no code change** — its `Program.cs` (checked at release `v0.2.1-beta.9`) already routes every non-`run` verb to `IntropyGenerate.RunAsync`, so once a host references the new package, `-- graph` just works. What remains is purely versioning:

1. Merge PR #3 and publish the `Intropy.Topology.*` packages.
2. Bump the template skeleton's csproj pins (currently `Version="0.2.0"` — that version emits the old apiVersion-less JSON, which the dashboard's decoder rejects by design) and cut a template release.
3. Your existing system host was scaffolded against 0.2.0, so bump the `Intropy.Topology.Aspire`/`.Generation` versions in its csproj by hand.

Reviewing the PR also surfaced two mismatches with what I'd built on the CLI side, both now fixed and verified:

- **Invocation**: the PR documents that plain `dotnet run` leaks build/launch-profile messages onto stdout (and the template ships a `launchSettings.json`, so it would). The provider now runs `dotnet build <host> -v q` first, then `dotnet run --no-build --no-launch-profile --project <host> -- graph`, with build failures reported separately from verb failures.
- **Kind casing**: the library kebab-cases component kinds (`TransactionalIntegration` → `transactional-integration`), which the flow view's icon lookup would have missed; it now normalizes hyphens.

Otherwise the PR matches the contract the dashboard expects exactly — camelCase with `pubsub` keys, `apiVersion`/`kind` constants, empty collections omitted, `port` dropped when `"default"`, file transport mapped to `{type: "file", supportsInput/Output: true}`. Full Go suite and the web build are green on `feature/dashboard-v2`, placeholder bundle restored.

Everything is still uncommitted on the branch — this would be a good moment to commit (either the 4-step series I proposed earlier, or one port commit now that the verb contract is settled). Want me to stage it?

Should we do anything about these? 
- Invocation: the PR documents that plain dotnet run leaks build/launch-profile messages onto stdout (and the template ships a launchSettings.json, so it would). The provider now runs dotnet build <host> -v q first, then dotnet run --no-build --no-launch-profile --project <host> -- graph, with build failures reported separately from verb failures.
- Kind casing: the library kebab-cases component kinds (TransactionalIntegration → transactional-integration), which the flow view's icon lookup would have missed; it now normalizes hyphens.

content.text:
No action needed — both are already fixed, tested, and sitting in the `feature/dashboard-v2` working tree from the previous step:

- **Invocation**: `internal/dashboard/topology.go` now runs `dotnet build <host> -v q` first, then `dotnet run --no-build --no-launch-profile --project <host> -- graph`, with build failures and verb failures reported as distinct errors. CONTRIBUTING.md documents the same invocation. This is also the *right* layer to fix it: the build/launch-profile noise comes from MSBuild before the app even starts, so the library can't suppress it — the consumer has to invoke it cleanly, which is exactly what PR #3's README prescribes.
- **Kind casing**: `FlowView.tsx`'s `dataFlowFor` now strips hyphens as well as case, so `transactional-integration` resolves to the right glyph. Worst case if it hadn't: a generic icon, never wrong wiring — the map is icon-only.

Both are covered by the green test runs from that turn, so they'll ride along in the port commit.

One optional loose end if you want belt-and-braces: the v1 contract doesn't formally pin the `kind` vocabulary casing — my Go type comment says `transactionalIntegration` (camelCase) while PR #3 emits kebab-case. The dashboard now tolerates both, but a one-line note on PR #3 (or in the library README) declaring kebab-case as canonical would prevent a third variant appearing later. I can also align the Go comment to match — say the word.

Meanwhile I paused mid-task on your NuGet bump: I found the PR branch checkout at `~/dev/intropy/tooling/intropy-topology` (`feat/system-host-graph-verb`, up to date with the PR head) and your local feed at `~/dev/intropy/local-nuget` (currently at 0.2.4). Next step would be packing that checkout as 0.2.5 into the feed and bumping your `OrderFlow.SystemHost.csproj` under `customers/fluxia/.../order-flow/system-host` to it. Want me to continue with that?

Done — the catalog now shows the system as a parent group. Your components report `system: "order-flow"`, which the sidebar already knows how to render as a collapsible parent node (with icon and count) above `order-extractor` and `order-loader`.

How it works: the server derives membership from the sibling `system-host` scaffold — the host's directory marks the system root, its recorded `values.name` provides the display name, and every block scaffolded next to it is grouped under that name. This is scaffold-record-driven (no dotnet involved), it kicks in even when the workspace root *is* the system root (your layout, where the old folder heuristic produced nothing), and a declared name also overrides the folder-derived name in nested layouts while the domain level stays folder-derived. Two new tests cover the flat and nested cases; the folder heuristic remains the fallback for workspaces without a host.

A bonus effect: the flow view's system dropdown will now label your group "order-flow" instead of the generic "Workspace".
